comparison: Use the finite real expansion with frequencies one through K, one cosine and one sine coefficient per frequency, each basis function divided by sqrt(pi). This gives exactly 2K real coefficients and no constant mode, with mean zero and the standing K>=2 restriction retained. The inspected Fourier basis is complex exponential and orthonormal under normalized Haar measure, whereas the source real trigonometric basis is orthonormal for ordinary Lebesgue integration on [-pi,pi). Passing between them requires both conjugate-frequency pairing and the measure/basis normalization factors; its coefficient vector cannot be substituted unchanged. Finite sums and real trigonometric functions construct the source expansion directly, with no infinite-series convergence issue.

comparison: Take the squared Euclidean distance from the estimated coefficient vector to the orbit of the true vector under the one-parameter frequency-weighted circle action. The orbit is nonempty and compact as a continuous image of the circle, so the inspected compact-set distance theorem supplies attainment and squaring preserves the minimizer because distances are nonnegative. The half-open angle representative interval is not itself compact; use its circle quotient or the compact orbit when justifying a minimum. Do not independently align phases at each frequency, substitute the coordinate supremum metric, divide by 2K, or assert uniqueness of the minimizing rotation in the presence of stabilizers.

comparison: Construct independent latent angles with normalized Lebesgue law on [-pi,pi) and independent standard Gaussian noise vectors in Euclidean 2K-space, independent also across samples, then push forward by rotated signal plus the fixed known positive sigma times noise. Normalized restriction via cond expresses the angle law because the interval has finite positive Lebesgue mass. Conditional on each angle the observation is Gaussian with mean g(alpha) theta and covariance sigma squared times identity; after integrating out the angle it is generally a Gaussian mixture, not one Gaussian vector. Preserve N independent observations, the full 2K coordinates and one shared angle per observation, rather than assigning independent angles to frequencies or estimating sigma by default.

comparison: Set the Gaussian density's mean parameter to mu and its nonnegative variance parameter to sigma squared. For sigma>0, its normalization 1/sqrt(2*pi*sigma squared) and exponent -(x-mu)^2/(2*sigma squared) agree with (1/sigma) phi((x-mu)/sigma). The library argument is variance, not standard deviation. Preserve the centered abbreviation phi_sigma where used later. The zero-scale Gaussian law is a Dirac measure and has no such Lebesgue density; the library's total density expression at zero variance must not silently extend this positive-scale kernel. No mixture distribution or prior is part of the single-kernel definition.
